desc: Security Enhanced Linux Policy for the hwloc_dhwd processes
r: hwloc_dhwd_selinux - Security Enhanced Linux Policy for the hwloc_dhwd processes

Security-Enhanced Linux secures the hwloc_dhwd processes via flexible mandatory access control.

The hwloc_dhwd processes execute with the hwloc_dhwd_t SELinux type. You can check if you have these processes running by executing the ps command with the -Z qualifier.

For example:

ps -eZ | grep hwloc_dhwd_t

The hwloc_dhwd_t SELinux type can be entered via the hwloc_dhwd_exec_t file type.

The default entrypoint paths for the hwloc_dhwd_t domain are the following:

/usr/sbin/hwloc-dump-hwdata

SELinux defines process types (domains) for each process running on the system

You can see the context of a process using the -Z option to ps

Policy governs the access confined processes have to files. SELinux hwloc_dhwd policy is very flexible allowing users to setup their hwloc_dhwd processes in as secure a method as possible.

The following process types are defined for hwloc_dhwd:

hwloc_dhwd_t

Note: semanage permissive -a hwloc_dhwd_t can be used to make the process type hwloc_dhwd_t permissive. SELinux does not deny access to permissive process types, but the AVC (SELinux denials) messages are still generated.

SELinux policy is customizable based on least access required. hwloc_dhwd policy is extremely flexible and has several booleans that allow you to manipulate the policy and run hwloc_dhwd with the tightest access possible.

If you want to allow all domains to execute in fips_mode, you must turn on the fips_mode boolean. Enabled by default.

setsebool -P fips_mode 1

The SELinux process type hwloc_dhwd_t can manage files labeled with the following file types. The paths listed are the default paths for these file types. Note the processes UID still need to have DAC permissions.

hwloc_var_run_t

/var/run/hwloc(/.*)?

SELinux requires files to have an extended attribute to define the file type.

You can see the context of a file using the -Z option to ls

Policy governs the access confined processes have to these files. SELinux hwloc_dhwd policy is very flexible allowing users to setup their hwloc_dhwd processes in as secure a method as possible.

STANDARD FILE CONTEXT

SELinux defines the file context types for the hwloc_dhwd, if you wanted to store files with these types in a different paths, you need to execute the semanage command to specify alternate labeling and then use restorecon to put the labels on disk.

semanage fcontext -a -t hwloc_dhwd_unit_t '/srv/myhwloc_dhwd_content(/.*)?'
restorecon -R -v /srv/myhwloc_dhwd_content

Note: SELinux often uses regular expressions to specify labels that match multiple files.

The following file types are defined for hwloc_dhwd:

hwloc_dhwd_exec_t

- Set files with the hwloc_dhwd_exec_t type, if you want to transition an executable to the hwloc_dhwd_t domain.

hwloc_dhwd_unit_t

- Set files with the hwloc_dhwd_unit_t type, if you want to treat the files as hwloc dhwd unit data.

Note: File context can be temporarily modified with the chcon command. If you want to permanently change the file context you need to use the semanage fcontext command. This will modify the SELinux labeling database. You will need to use restorecon to apply the labels.

semanage fcontext can also be used to manipulate default file context mappings.

semanage permissive can also be used to manipulate whether or not a process type is permissive.

semanage module can also be used to enable/disable/install/remove policy modules.

semanage boolean can also be used to manipulate the booleans

system-config-selinux is a GUI tool available to customize SELinux policy settings.
